title: Work backward to the original whole
subtitle: Percentages · 9 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **9 of the official questions in Percentages are this one** — 1 Easy, 4 Medium, 4 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The part is given and the whole is unknown.
- Look for phrasing like 'A is p% of what number', 'after increasing x by p% the result is R', or 'the remaining n people make up the rest'.
- The number you know is the result, and the question asks for the starting value.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Write an equation with the unknown whole: (decimal) × x = known value.
- For an increase, use (1 + r)·x = result; for a decrease, use (1 − r)·x = result.
- 2) Divide the known value by the multiplier.
- 3) If there is a leftover group, first work out its percent as 100 minus the listed percents, then solve for the total, then answer the actual follow-up question.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type the equation with x, for example 1.2x=150.
Desmos draws a vertical line and shows the x-value.
This avoids dividing the wrong way.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You take p% of the given number instead of dividing by the multiplier.
For example, you shrink the result by p% to 'undo' an increase, which gives the wrong starting value.
With a leftover group, you might stop at the total and never answer the follow-up.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You take p% of the given number instead of dividing by the multiplier.
For example, you shrink the result by p% to 'undo' an increase, which gives the wrong starting value.
